column1: # Traduzione inglese dei testi del corso Tongji (lezioni 19-25 e primi esercizi).

column2: I didn’t prepare well.
A goodbye formula for someone who is leaving (“go slowly, take care”). The person leaving says 我先走了.
I’m off, let’s talk another time. — Bye, take care!
Adjective + 极了 · 这么 + adjective
极了 = extremely; 这么 = so, so much.
It’s incredibly hot today.
Why are you in such a hurry?
At the clinic
Doctor
What’s the matter?
I have a headache and a bit of a cough.
Do you have a fever?
I had a fever last night, today it’s a bit better.
You’ve caught a cold, it’s not serious.
I have an exam tomorrow: can I go?
Yes. Go home today, get some proper rest and drink plenty of water.
Thank you, doctor! I’ll be going then.
Goodbye, take care!
Lisa is better

Last week Lisa was very ill: fever and a cough, and for three days she didn’t go to class. Annie went with her to the hospital every day and also bought her food. Ms Tian and her classmates were all worried about her. Now Lisa is much better and says: “Thank you all for your concern! Now I’ll work hard to revise for the end-of-semester exams.”
Red beans grow in the south: in spring, how many sprigs come out? Please gather plenty of them: nothing speaks of longing more than they do.
What’s your hobby?
Hobbies, sport and free time; listing activities; causes and consequences
In speech, 啦 after each item is used to list several activities or things, with a lively tone.
In the evening I usually do my homework, listen to recordings, prepare the new lesson…
真是 + (一)个 + noun expresses a strong judgement: “you really are a…”.
You really are a good teacher!
As an adverb: “almost” (差不多每天 = almost every day). As an adjective: “more or less the same”.
I go to the mountains almost every weekend.
His level of Chinese is more or less the same as mine.
更 (even more)
更 + adjective / verb: an even higher degree. It is also used with 比.
I like sport, and table tennis even more.
A taxi is even faster than the bus.
因为 introduces the cause, 所以 the consequence (you can also use just one of the two).
Because it was raining, we didn’t go to the mountains.
一般 · 打 + ball
一般 = usually. With ball games you use 打: 打乒乓球, 打篮球.
At the weekend I usually go shopping.
Can you play table tennis?
Weekend plans
I like listening to music and singing. What’s your hobby?
I love sport: basketball, hiking, cycling…
You’re amazing!
This weekend I’m going hiking in the Western Hills: are you coming too?
I’m not very keen on hiking. How about going to sing together?
OK: Saturday hiking, Sunday karaoke!
So your weekend will be even more tiring!
Li Wenjing’s hobbies

Li Wenjing has lots of hobbies: she likes reading, listening to music and sport too. She is on the school basketball team and trains for an hour almost every afternoon. At the weekend she usually goes round the shops nearby with her friends. She says: “Shopping isn’t tiring: studying is more tiring!”
春夜喜雨 · 杜甫 (first verse)
The good rain knows its season: it comes just in spring. It follows the wind and slips into the night, soaking everything, fine and silent.
How to address people

With strangers: 先生 for a man; 阿姨 or 大姐 for a woman, depending on age; 小朋友 for children; 师傅 for taxi drivers, workers, cooks. With acquaintances: surname + title (李老师, 王大夫), or 小 + surname for someone younger (小王) and 老 + surname for someone older (老张).
At eight I was in class
Telling when, where and how something happened; actions in progress; studying characters
For an action that has already happened, 是……的 highlights WHEN, WHERE, HOW or WITH WHOM it happened. 是 can be left out in statements, but not in negatives (不是……的).
When did you come to China? — Last year.
I came by train, not by plane.
Shows an action in progress at a given moment, also in the past: “I was doing”.
When you arrived I was reading.
A modest reply to a compliment: “oh no, not at all”. Often repeated: 哪里哪里.
Your Chinese has improved a lot! — Oh, not really.
“As long as… then…”: the condition is enough to get the result.
As long as you read the text every day, you’ll memorise the new words.
“About to…”: 快 + verb / time + 了.
Class is about to end.
It’ll be the weekend soon!
不要 + verb = don’t… (prohibition); 跟 + person + (一起) + verb = with someone; 最 + adjective = the most.
Don’t just look at the pinyin.
Practise calligraphy with me.
My biggest problem is the characters.
A new classmate
Hi! Are you the new classmate?
Yes, I arrived last week.
Where are you from?
I’m from Korea.
Had you studied Chinese before?
Yes, for a year, at university. But I know very few characters.
Don’t worry: just read the text every day and you’ll memorise them.
You really speak Chinese well!
Oh, not really. Class is about to start, let’s go!
A missed call

Yesterday at eight in the evening Wang Ping called Annie, but she didn’t answer because she was studying in the library. She only noticed at half past nine, back in the dorm. She called Wang Ping back: “Sorry, I was studying earlier. What’s up?” Wang Ping answered: “Nothing special, I wanted to ask whether you’ve prepared for tomorrow’s dictation.”

The lamp lit at midnight, the cock crowing at dawn: this is just the time for the young to study. Whoever, with black hair, does not know to study early and hard, with a white head will regret having studied too late.
Back from the trip
Talking about a trip, distances, actions in sequence and at the same time, Chinese meals
“First… then…”: two actions in sequence (usually future or habitual).
First let’s go to the library, then to the canteen.
Two actions done at the same time by the same person.
I often eat while looking at my phone.
A rhetorical question expressing surprise: “didn’t you say…? / aren’t you…?”.
Weren’t you off on your trip? Why are you still here?
“To think (wrongly)”: you believed one thing, but reality is different.
I thought you were Japanese, but you’re Korean!
离 (distance)
A 离 B + 远 / 近, or A 离 B + (有) + distance.
The dorm is close to the classrooms.
That place is more than ten kilometres from the school.
得 děi + verb
“Must, have to” (spoken). Careful: the same character is read de (complement: 说得很好) and dé (to get: 得了感冒).
The canteen is about to close: we have to hurry.
俩 = 两个 (people): 我们俩. 刚 (adverb) goes before the verb; 刚才 (“just now”) is a time expression and can also go before the subject.
Let’s go together, the two of us.
I’ve just arrived, I haven’t eaten yet.
Back from Xi’an
Peter, you’re back from your trip! How was it?
Great fun!
Where did you go?
I went to Xi’an, by train.
Is Xi’an far from here?
Quite far: it takes more than five hours by train.
Did you go on your own?
No, with Liu Wei. We travelled and practised speaking at the same time.
Great! Have you had dinner yet?
Not yet. I’ve just got back: first I’ll rest a bit, then I’ll go and eat.
A trip to the mountains

Last weekend Annie and her friends went to a place more than thirty kilometres from the school, where the mountains are beautiful. They went by bus, chatting and listening to music along the way. At noon they had a Chinese lunch in a small restaurant and at the end they also ate lots of fruit. In the evening, on the way back, they were all tired, but they’d had a great time.
At the Qingming festival the rain falls thick; the travellers on the road are heartbroken. “Where can I find a tavern?” I ask; the shepherd boy points far off to the village of apricot blossoms.
The courses of a Chinese meal

At a lunch or dinner with guests you usually start with cold dishes (凉菜) and drinks, then come the hot dishes (热菜) and rice; the soup often comes towards the end and the meal finishes with fruit. In southern China, however, soup is also served at the beginning.
What should I wear?
Clothes and sizes, the weather forecast, trying on and choosing, giving up
还是 (still, all the same)
After an attempt, 还是 + verb / adjective shows that the situation doesn’t change: “still, all the same”.
I said it twice, but he still doesn’t understand.
“Forget it, never mind”: you give something up.
No large size? Never mind, I won’t buy it.
一 + MW + 比 + 一 + MW
Expresses a progression: “more and more…”. 一天比一天 = day by day.
His Chinese is getting better day by day.
There are more new words with every lesson.
没有一 + MW + …的
“Not a single one”: 没有一双合适的 = there isn’t a single pair in the right size.
Not one pair of these shoes fits.
Corrects the cause or interpretation: “it’s not that…, it’s that…”.
It’s not that this dress is expensive: it’s that I didn’t bring any money.
“When…, then…”: the action is put off until later.
I’ll go and buy it when I have time.
最……的了 · adjectives for clothes
最 + adjective + 的了 = “it’s the most… there is”. For clothes: 大 / 小, 长 / 短, 肥 (loose) / 瘦 (tight), 合适 (right).
This is the largest size there is.
These trousers are a bit short.
In the shoe shop
These shoes look really nice: may I try them on?
Of course. What size are you?
These are a 38, try them on.
They’re a bit tight. Do you have a slightly bigger size?
How about these, size 39?
They’re still not right: they’re a bit big.
Then try this model: it fits a little smaller.
Sorry for the trouble! … These are perfect.
No trouble at all.
Yamada’s down jacket

The forecast says it will be colder tomorrow than today, and windy at night too. Yamada has only brought a coat, which isn’t very warm. He goes to a shop to buy a down jacket. He tries on three: the first is too short, the second too loose, the third is an ugly colour. In the end he says: “Never mind, I’ll come back and buy it at the weekend.”

A year ago, on this very day, behind this door, her face and the peach blossoms lent each other their pink. Now I don’t know where that face has gone; the peach blossoms, as before, smile in the spring wind.
Who is in your family?
Family, jobs, school; photos and family likenesses
上 + school
上 also means “to attend” a school or start a regular activity: 上小学, 上中学, 上大学, 上班.
My younger brother is at high school.
“Obviously! It goes without saying!”: a rhetorical question of confirmation.
Do you like Chinese food? — Obviously!
全 + noun
全 (whole, entire) goes directly before the noun, without 的: 全家, 全班, 全校, 全世界.
The whole class went.
像 (to look like)
A 像 B = A looks like B. For appearance: A 长得(很)像 B.
He has his father’s eyes.
You look a lot like your brother.
The family: 口
你家有几口人? / 你家有什么人? The measure word for family members is 口.
There are four of us in my family: dad, mum, my brother and me.
会 + verb + 的 expresses a confident prediction: “will definitely…”.
You’ll definitely like this place.
Liu Wei’s family
Liu Wei, how many people are there in your family?
Four: dad, mum, my younger brother and me.
What do your parents do?
My father teaches at a high school, my mother works in a hospital: she’s a doctor.
And your brother?
He’s at high school, next year he’ll take the university entrance exam.
Do you have a photo of the whole family?
Yes, look, here it is.
Your brother really looks like you!
Everyone says so.
Yamada’s family

There are five people in Yamada’s family: his grandfather, his grandmother, his father, his mother and him. His father is a lawyer and is very busy; his mother is a shop assistant. Yamada is a university student and graduates next year. After graduating he wants to come to China to do a master’s degree. He says: “Everyone at home is very welcoming: if you go to Japan, you must come and visit us!”
秋浦歌 · 李白 (no. 15)
White hair three thousand zhang long: that is how long my sorrow is. I don’t know where, in the bright mirror, this autumn frost has come from.
How will you spend the winter holidays?
Holiday plans, Chinese festivals, booking tickets, giving good wishes
“As soon as…, (right away)…”: the second action immediately follows the first. The subjects can be the same or different.
As soon as he got back to the dorm he went to sleep.
This character is easy: I understand it at first glance.
元旦 and 春节

元旦 is 1 January, New Year in the solar calendar. 春节 is the first day of the first lunar month (between late January and February): it is the most important traditional festival, when people go back to their 老家 to celebrate with their family.
For the Spring Festival I’m going back to my hometown.
Indefinite 什么
什么 can mean “something / nothing in particular”, without asking a question.
Do you need to buy anything?
You don’t need to bring anything.
好几 + measure word
“Several, quite a few”: before a number/measure word or time words.
I waited several hours.
I want to go to quite a few places.
Strengthens the condition: “if…”. Often with 就 in the second part.
If it’s convenient, bring some fruit.
或者 and 还是
Both mean “or”: 或者 is used in statements, 还是 in questions.
You can take the train or the plane.
Are you taking the train or the plane?
然后 = then, afterwards (links two actions in sequence); number + 左右 = about; 祝 + good wishes.
First we’ll eat, then we’ll go to the cinema.
I’m planning to stay about a week.
Happy New Year and good health to everyone!
An invitation for the Spring Festival
Yamada, are you going back to Japan for the winter holidays?
Yes. But first I’d like to spend the Spring Festival in China, and then go back.
Then come and celebrate in my hometown! My parents will be delighted.
Really? Fantastic! Where is your hometown?
In Yunnan, not far from Kunming.
Should I bring any presents?
You don’t need anything. Book your plane ticket soon, though: they’re hard to get for the Spring Festival.
OK, I’ll check online this evening.
If there are any problems, give me a call.
Lisa’s plans

(Lisa tells us) As soon as the end-of-semester exams are over I’m going travelling. I’ve already booked the train to Xi’an on 20 January. I’m thinking of staying in Xi’an for about five days, then I’ll go to Shanghai to celebrate the Spring Festival with friends. After the Festival I’ll go home. Happy New Year, everyone!

At dawn I leave Baidi among coloured clouds; a thousand li to Jiangling, and I’m back in a day. From both banks the cries of the monkeys never stop, and the light boat has already passed ten thousand mountains.
Small talk

Chinese people often greet each other with questions: 吃了吗？ (have you eaten?), 去哪儿？ (where are you going?), 最近忙吗？, or by commenting on what the other person is doing (上课去呀？). They are polite formulas: you answer briefly (吃了 / 还可以 / 出去一下). 改天聊聊 or 有空儿来玩儿 when saying goodbye are also courtesies, not real invitations: a real invitation gives a day and a time.
It’s too expensive!
太贵了 = it’s too expensive.
Wait a moment, please.
等 = to wait.
什么 = what.
My name is Jeff.
叫 + name = to be called.
My surname is Tian, I’m your teacher.
姓 + surname.
I’m Chinese, and you?
呢 repeats the question: “and you?”.
都 = all, before the verb.
She is our teacher.
的 shows possession.
Good morning, Ms Tian! (polite)
您 is the polite form of 你.
Are you American?
吗 at the end of a sentence = yes/no question.
I’m English, he’s English too.
也 = also, before the verb.
几 asks for a small number.
I’m twenty this year.
岁 = years of age.
How old are you?
多大 asks someone’s age.
What nationality are you?
哪国人 = from which country.
Who is he?
是 = to be.
半 = half.
It’s five to ten.
差 + minutes + hour = … to …
从……到…… = from… to…
It’s two o’clock now.
Before 点 you use 两, not 二.
The negative of 有 is 没有.
该……了 = it’s time to…
What day of the week is it today?
星期几 asks for the day.
请问 introduces a polite question.
不用谢 = you’re welcome.
Reference point + 的 + 旁边.
Adjective as predicate: 很 + adjective, without 是.
Excuse me, where is the class 3 classroom?
哪儿 = where?
The toilet isn’t here, it’s there.
这儿 = here, 那儿 = there.
How much is this bicycle?
辆 is the measure word for vehicles.
I bought two books.
本 is the measure word for books.
A pair of shoes costs 120 yuan.
双 = pair.
There are both black ones and blue ones.
都 sums up the items listed before.
I want this one, and that one as well.
还 = also, in addition.
Which colour do you like?
种 = kind, type.
I bought a piece of clothing.
Verb + 了 = completed action.
怎么样 asks for an opinion.
Hello, is that Wang Ping?
喂 is used to start or answer a phone call.
吧 at the end of a sentence = suggestion.
I’m calling him.
给 + person + verb.
祝 = to wish.
